Evaluation, with and without ground truth

Source: vignettes/articles/evaluation.Rmd
evaluation.Rmd

Once you have a clustering, you need to judge it. The tools differ depending on whether you have a known grouping to compare against. This page covers both cases, and how to compare methods against each other.

library(MosaiClusteR)
data(mosaic_toy)
L     <- mosaic_toy$List
truth <- mosaic_toy$truth
fit   <- SNF(L, type = "data", distmeasure = rep("euclidean", length(L)),
             normalize = rep(FALSE, length(L)), method = rep(list(NULL), length(L)))
lab   <- mosaic_labels(fit, 3)

With ground truth

When you know the true grouping (a benchmark, a simulation, a validated subtype), cluster_agreement() scores a clustering against it with four complementary measures:

cluster_agreement(lab, truth)   # ARI, NMI, Jaccard, purity
  • ARI (Adjusted Rand Index): agreement on which pairs share a cluster, corrected for chance. The headline number.
  • NMI (Normalised Mutual Information): shared information between the two labellings.
  • Jaccard: overlap of co-membership, uncorrected for chance.
  • Purity: how cleanly each cluster maps to a single true group.

Rule of thumb for ARI: above 0.90 excellent, 0.75 to 0.90 good, 0.50 to 0.75 moderate, below 0.50 weak. All of ARI, NMI and Jaccard return 1 for identical partitions up to relabelling, including the single-cluster and all-singleton cases, and missing labels raise a clear error rather than a cryptic one.

Labels are arbitrary names, so before comparing two solutions by eye, align one to the other with ReorderToReference():

ReorderToReference(reference = truth, tocompare = lab)

Without ground truth

On real data you usually have no truth to compare against. Judge a clustering by how well separated it is and by how reliably it reproduces.

Internal separation. The silhouette measures how much better each object fits its own cluster than the nearest other cluster. CompareSilCluster() compares candidate solutions by silhouette, and cluster_k_sweep() reports silhouette and within-dispersion across k.

CompareSilCluster(fit$DistM, nrclusters = 2:6)

Single source versus multi-source. CompareSvsM() contrasts a single-source clustering with the integrated one, which shows whether integration actually added structure over the best single source.

Stability. A solution you cannot reproduce is not worth interpreting. Re-run a stochastic method with different seeds, or subsample the objects, and check that the labels agree with cluster_agreement(). The stability checks in the choosing-k guide apply directly here.

Comparing two integrations

compare_clusterings() clusters two dissimilarities at the same k and reports their agreement, so you can ask how much two methods actually differ:

fit_a <- ADC(L, distmeasure = "euclidean", normalize = FALSE)
compare_clusterings(fit_a$DistM, fit$DistM, NC = 3)   # ARI, NMI, Jaccard + crosstab

clustering_concordance() summarises agreement across several solutions at once, and compare_methods_plot() and ComparePlot() show the solutions side by side so disagreements are visible, not just numeric.

A comparison-first workflow

Because every method shares one interface, the recommended practice is to run several, score them the same way, and prefer structure that reproduces:

methods <- list(
  ADC = function() mosaic_labels(ADC(L, distmeasure = "euclidean", normalize = FALSE), 3),
  SNF = function() mosaic_labels(fit, 3),
  ABC = function() mosaic_labels(M_ABC(L, NC = 3, seed = 1), 3)
)
sapply(methods, function(f) cluster_agreement(f(), truth)[["ARI"]])

With a known truth, read the ARI column. Without one, lean on silhouette and on agreement across methods and seeds.
